title: Advanced Grammar & Syntax
description: Beyond the basics — complex sentences, subordination, tense control, modal verbs, linking ideas and paragraphing for effect.

notes.heading: Complex Sentences and Subordination
notes.body: You already know simple sentences (one main verb: 'He walked home') and compound sentences (two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction or semicolon: 'He walked home, but she stayed'). A complex sentence goes further: it combines one main (independent) clause with one or more subordinate (dependent) clauses. A subordinate clause cannot stand alone — 'because the bus was late' leaves the reader hanging; it only makes sense attached to a main clause: 'Amara missed assembly because the bus was late.' Subordination is the skill of showing which idea matters most: the main clause carries the core message, the subordinate clause adds reason, time, condition or contrast. Compare 'The match was cancelled. It rained.' (two flat simple sentences) with 'The match was cancelled because it rained.' (the cause is now built into the sentence). Subordinate clauses can also be introduced by relative pronouns (who, which, that, whose): 'The girl who won the race smiled.' Common pitfall: writing a subordinate clause as a full sentence ('Because I was tired.') — that is a fragment, not a sentence. Exam tip: markers at Y8/Y9 actively look for controlled complex sentences, so aim to include several per paragraph of extended writing.

notes.heading: Subordinating Conjunctions and the Comma Rule
notes.body: Subordinating conjunctions are the words that attach a subordinate clause to a main clause. Learn them by job: time (when, before, after, until, once, whenever, while), cause (because, since, as), condition (if, unless, even if), contrast or concession (although, even though, whereas, despite). A useful memory set is 'A WHITE BUS': Although/As, When/While/Whenever/Whereas, If, Though, Even though, Because, Until/Unless, Since/So that. The crucial punctuation rule: when the subordinate clause comes FIRST, separate it from the main clause with a comma — 'Although it was dark, Lily kept walking.' When the main clause comes first, you normally need no comma — 'Lily kept walking although it was dark.' The same logic applies mid-sentence, where the clause is wrapped in paired commas: 'Lily, although it was dark, kept walking.' Do not confuse subordinating with coordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) — coordinators join equals, subordinators join unequal ideas. Quick check: if you can move the clause to the front of the sentence and it still works, it is subordinate: 'Because he was late, he ran' = 'He ran because he was late.'

notes.heading: Linking Ideas Within and Across Sentences
notes.body: Good writing guides the reader from one idea to the next, and connectives are the signposts. Within a sentence you link with conjunctions; across sentences you link with conjunctive adverbs — words and phrases like 'however', 'therefore', 'consequently', 'furthermore', 'nevertheless', 'meanwhile', 'in contrast'. Each signals a different relationship: addition (furthermore, moreover, also), contrast (however, nevertheless, on the other hand), cause and result (therefore, consequently, as a result), time (meanwhile, afterwards), and example (for instance). Punctuation matters: a conjunctive adverb joining two complete sentences needs a semicolon before it and a comma after — 'The evidence was weak; therefore, the case collapsed.' Using just a comma there ('The evidence was weak, therefore the case collapsed') is a comma splice, a common error. Choose connectives precisely: 'however' and 'therefore' are not interchangeable — one signals contrast, the other result. Also vary your links: starting every sentence with 'Also...' or 'But...' reads mechanically, so sometimes embed the link mid-sentence ('The results, however, told a different story'). In analytical essays, accurate connectives show the examiner your argument is logically organised, not just a list of points.

notes.heading: Tense Control: Past vs Present
notes.body: Tense tells the reader when something happens, and controlling it is a mark of mature writing. Past tense ('she opened the door') is the natural choice for storytelling and recounting events — it mirrors how we tell stories in conversation. Present tense ('she opens the door') makes events feel immediate, as if unfolding now, and is the standard choice for essays and analysis: when you write about a text, convention says the text 'lives' in the present — 'Shakespeare presents Macbeth as ambitious', not 'presented'. Future tense ('she will open the door') appears in plans, predictions and introductions ('This essay will argue...'). The golden rule is consistency: pick a tense for a piece or section and stay in it unless you have a reason to shift (a flashback, a prediction). The most common error is accidental drift: 'Romeo enters the tomb and saw Juliet lying there.' Fix it by proofreading each verb. Deliberate shifts are powerful, though: a narrative written in past tense can switch to present for a climactic moment to heighten drama. Watch irregular verbs and the verb 'to be' especially: singular past is 'was' (I/he/she was), plural and 'you' take 'were'.

notes.heading: Modal Verbs: Certainty, Possibility and Obligation
notes.body: Modal verbs are helper verbs that sit before a main verb and colour its meaning — they express possibility, ability, permission, obligation or prediction rather than time alone. The core set: can/could, may/might, shall/should, will/would, must, ought to. They never change form (no 'musts' or 'might-ed') and are always followed by the bare infinitive ('she might go', never 'she might goes'). Think of them as a dial of certainty: 'It will rain' (certain) → 'It should rain' (probable) → 'It might rain' (possible). The same dial works for obligation: 'You must finish' is a command, 'You should finish' is advice, 'You could finish' is an option. Modals are a precision tool in persuasive and formal writing: 'The council must act now' sounds far more urgent than 'The council could act.' Common pitfalls: writing 'would of' instead of 'would have' (the contraction 'would've' fools the ear), and double modals ('might could') which are non-standard in formal English. In analysis, quoting a writer's modal verbs is a sharp way to discuss tone — a character who says 'I might stay' is hedging; one who says 'I will stay' is resolute.

notes.heading: Paragraphing: Organising Ideas
notes.body: A paragraph is a group of sentences built around one idea, starting on a new line. Paragraphs exist for the reader: they break text into digestible chunks and signal when you have moved to a new point, time, place, speaker or topic. A solid paragraph often has a recognisable shape: a topic sentence that states the paragraph's main idea, supporting sentences that develop it with detail, evidence or examples, and a final sentence that rounds off or links forward to the next paragraph. In essays, one new point = one new paragraph; in narratives, start a new paragraph for a change of time, place, action or speaker. Common mistakes: paragraphs that sprawl over several unrelated ideas, single-sentence fragments everywhere (which looks disjointed), and no paragraphs at all — a wall of text that loses the reader instantly. Check your work by reading just the first sentence of each paragraph: those topic sentences alone should sketch the skeleton of your whole argument or story. In exams, clear paragraphing is one of the fastest ways to show an examiner that your writing is organised and purposeful.

notes.heading: Using Grammar Deliberately for Effect
notes.body: At this level grammar stops being a set of rules to obey and becomes a set of choices to exploit. Sentence variety is the big lever: a run of simple sentences ('The door creaked. He froze. Silence.') creates tension and pace, while long, multi-clause sentences slow the reader down and suit description or complex reasoning — skilled writers alternate the two deliberately. The same logic applies to paragraphs: a one-line paragraph after several long ones ('Then the lights went out.') lands like a drumbeat because contrast makes it stand out. Where you place information matters too: fronting a subordinate clause ('Exhausted but unbeaten, the team walked off') builds suspense before the main clause arrives. Tense can be a tool — switching a past-tense narrative into the present at the climax pulls the reader into the moment. Even the passive voice, usually best avoided, earns its place when the doer is unknown, irrelevant or deliberately hidden: 'The window had been broken.' The exam skill is not just doing these things but being able to name and explain them: when analysing a text, comment on how sentence length, clause order and paragraph shape shape meaning and pace — that is what separates top-band analysis from simple feature-spotting.

flashcards.definition: A sentence with one main (independent) clause plus at least one subordinate clause that adds detail such as reason, time or condition.
flashcards.example: Amara missed assembly because the bus was late.

flashcards.definition: A clause that cannot stand alone as a sentence; it depends on a main clause to complete its meaning.
flashcards.example: 'Although it was dark' needs a main clause: 'Although it was dark, Lily kept walking.'

flashcards.definition: A word that attaches a subordinate clause to a main clause, showing time, cause, condition or contrast (because, although, if, when, unless).
flashcards.example: The match was cancelled because it rained.

flashcards.definition: When the subordinate clause comes first, follow it with a comma; when the main clause comes first, no comma is usually needed.
flashcards.example: 'If it rains, we will stay in' but 'We will stay in if it rains.'

flashcards.definition: A pronoun (who, which, that, whose) that introduces a subordinate clause describing a noun.
flashcards.example: The girl who won the race smiled.

flashcards.definition: A linking word that connects two complete sentences, showing result, contrast or addition (however, therefore, furthermore); use a semicolon before and a comma after.
flashcards.example: The evidence was weak; therefore, the case collapsed.

flashcards.definition: The error of joining two complete sentences with only a comma — fix it with a full stop, semicolon or conjunction.
flashcards.example: Wrong: 'It was late, we went home.' Right: 'It was late, so we went home.'

flashcards.definition: A helper verb expressing possibility, obligation, ability or prediction — can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must — followed by the bare infinitive.
Keeping one tense through a piece or section, shifting only for a deliberate reason such as a flashback or a moment of drama.
flashcards.example: Wrong: 'Romeo enters the tomb and saw Juliet.' Right: 'Romeo enters the tomb and sees Juliet.'

flashcards.definition: The convention of writing about texts and characters in the present tense, because the text 'lives' whenever it is read.
The sentence, usually first in a paragraph, that states the paragraph's main idea; the rest of the paragraph develops it.
flashcards.example: Reading a text's topic sentences alone should sketch the skeleton of the whole argument.

flashcards.definition: A very short paragraph used deliberately, usually after longer ones, to create emphasis, drama or a turning point.

choices: It contains two independent clauses joined by 'and'
It contains at least three verbs
It combines a main clause with at least one subordinate clause
It is longer than fifteen words
questions.explanation: A complex sentence is defined by structure, not length: one main clause plus a subordinate clause that cannot stand alone ('She left early because she felt ill'). Two independent clauses joined by 'and' make a compound sentence, and word count has nothing to do with it — 'Although tired, she ran' is complex at four words.

questions.stem: Which word is a subordinating conjunction?
choices: and
but
so
although
questions.explanation: 'Although' introduces a subordinate clause of concession: 'Although it rained, we played.' 'And', 'but' and 'so' are coordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS) — they join two clauses of equal status, which is compound structure, not subordination.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a modal verb?
choices: She sings beautifully
She might sing tonight
She sang yesterday
She is singing now
questions.explanation: 'Might' is a modal verb expressing possibility, followed by the bare infinitive 'sing'. The other sentences show ordinary tense forms — present, past simple and present continuous — with no modal colouring the meaning.

choices: The sentence that states the paragraph's main idea, usually at the start
The longest sentence in a paragraph
The first sentence of the whole essay
A sentence containing the title of the text
questions.explanation: A topic sentence introduces what the paragraph is about; the sentences after it develop that idea with detail or evidence. It is about function, not length, and each paragraph — not just the first — normally has one.

questions.stem: Why might a writer use a one-line paragraph like 'Then the lights went out.' after several long paragraphs?
choices: Because they ran out of things to say
To save space on the page
To create emphasis and drama through contrast
To signal a spelling section
questions.explanation: A lone short paragraph stands out against longer ones, so the reader slows down and feels its weight — it is a deliberate dramatic device, common at turning points in stories. It is a stylistic choice, not a sign of having nothing to say.

choices: Because the storm was close the harbour emptied
Because the storm was close, the harbour emptied
The harbour emptied, because the storm was close
Because, the storm was close the harbour emptied
questions.explanation: When the subordinate clause comes first, a comma separates it from the main clause: 'Because the storm was close, the harbour emptied.' When the main clause leads, no comma is needed, so choice C's comma before 'because' is wrong; choice A misses the required comma; choice D puts the comma after the conjunction itself.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Romeo enters the tomb and saw Juliet lying there.' Which version keeps the tense consistent?
choices: Romeo entered the tomb and sees Juliet lying there
Romeo will enter the tomb and saw Juliet lying there
Romeo enters the tomb and would see Juliet lying there
Romeo enters the tomb and sees Juliet lying there
questions.explanation: Analytical writing about a text uses the literary present throughout: 'enters... sees'. The original mixes present ('enters') with past ('saw'), and the other options repeat the same kind of mismatch between tenses. Consistency means every verb shares the chosen timeframe unless a shift is deliberate.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a conjunctive adverb correctly?
choices: The bridge was closed; therefore, we took the long way home
The bridge was closed, therefore we took the long way home
The bridge was closed therefore, we took the long way home
The bridge was closed therefore we took the long way home
questions.explanation: A conjunctive adverb joining two complete sentences needs a semicolon before it and a comma after: '; therefore,'. Joining with only a comma (choice B) is a comma splice, and omitting punctuation entirely (choices C and D) leaves the two sentences fused. A full stop plus a capital would also work.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'Although the storm raged, the sailors pressed on', which part is the subordinate clause?
choices: the sailors pressed on
the storm raged
Although the storm raged
the sailors
questions.explanation: A subordinate clause cannot stand alone, and 'Although the storm raged' leaves the reader waiting for the main point — it is the dependent clause, introduced by the subordinating conjunction 'although'. 'The sailors pressed on' is the main clause because it works as a complete sentence by itself. Choice B omits the conjunction that marks the clause as subordinate.

questions.stem: A headteacher wants a school rule to sound like a firm obligation, not a suggestion. Which sentence does this best?
choices: Pupils could arrive by 8:45
Pupils must arrive by 8:45
Pupils might arrive by 8:45
Pupils may arrive by 8:45
questions.explanation: Modal verbs dial obligation up and down: 'must' expresses a firm requirement, while 'could' and 'might' express mere possibility and 'may' grants permission. Choosing the right modal lets a writer control exactly how forceful a statement sounds — a key precision tool in formal writing.

questions.stem: Why do we conventionally write 'Shakespeare presents Macbeth as ambitious' rather than 'presented' in an essay?
choices: Because Shakespeare is still alive
Because past tense is always wrong in essays
Because 'presents' is easier to spell
Because a text 'lives' in the present whenever it is read, so analysis uses the literary present
questions.explanation: The literary present treats the events of a text as happening each time it is read, so analysis stays in the present tense. Past tense is not wrong in essays generally — it is correct for historical context ('Shakespeare wrote the play around 1606') — but the play's action and the writer's methods are described as present.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates a subordinate clause embedded in the middle of the main clause?
choices: Lily, who didn't like the dark, stayed at home
Lily who didn't like the dark, stayed at home
Lily, who didn't like the dark stayed at home
Lily who didn't like the dark stayed at home
questions.explanation: A subordinate clause dropped into the middle of a main clause is extra information, so it must be wrapped in a pair of commas — one before and one after: 'Lily, who didn't like the dark, stayed at home.' With only one comma (choices B and C) or none (choice D), the clause is not properly fenced off and the sentence misleads the reader about where the main clause resumes.

questions.stem: A writer wants to build suspense by making the reader wait for the main event. Which version does this most effectively?
choices: The team walked off the pitch. They were exhausted but unbeaten
The team walked off the pitch, and they were exhausted but unbeaten
Exhausted but unbeaten, the team walked off the pitch
The exhausted but unbeaten team walked off the pitch
questions.explanation: Fronting the subordinate element ('Exhausted but unbeaten,') delays the main clause, so the reader must wait for the key action — that delay is what creates suspense. The other versions state the main event immediately or demote the description to an adjective phrase, losing the build-up. Clause order is a deliberate tool for controlling pace.

questions.stem: A past-tense story suddenly switches to present tense at its climax: 'I ran all night. Now I am at the gate. It begins to open.' What is the most likely intended effect?
choices: It is an error — the writer lost control of tense
The shift makes the climax feel immediate, as if happening now, pulling the reader into the moment
The writer wants to show off their grammar knowledge
Present tense is required by the rules of fiction
questions.explanation: A deliberate tense shift at a key moment is a recognised technique: the present tense collapses the distance between reader and event, making the climax feel live. Because the shift is localised and purposeful (only at the climax), it is a choice, not a consistency error — accidental drift is random, not focused on the dramatic peak.

questions.stem: Which of these is a genuine reason to choose the passive voice deliberately?
choices: It always makes writing sound more exciting
It uses fewer words than the active voice
It is the required voice for all formal essays
The doer of the action is unknown or irrelevant, as in 'The window had been broken'
questions.explanation: The passive earns its place when the receiver of the action matters more than the doer — 'The castle was built in 1066' focuses on the castle, and 'The window had been broken' suits a writer who cannot or will not name who did it. It is not more exciting (usually the opposite), is wordier than the active, and no rule requires it in essays — it is a targeted choice, not a default.
